preamble: The voiced velar stop [ɡ] became the voiceless unaspirated palatal stop [c] in two unrelated cases, each combining palatalization with loss of voicing. In Lhasa Tibetan the written clusters with a g- base and -y- medial (Old Tibetan *ɡʲ) preceded by the prefixes b- or s- are pronounced [c] with low tone: brgya 'hundred' is /ca˩˨/ and brgyad 'eight' is /cɛː˩˧˨/. The velar was palatalized by the medial -y-, the prefix was lost and the old voiced stop devoiced as part of Lhasa tonogenesis; with the prefix r- the outcome is often still voiced [ɟ] (rgyal po 'king' /ɟɛː˩˨.poˑ/). In Icelandic, Old Norse g [ɡ] before front unrounded vowels is pronounced as the unaspirated palatal [c], as in gefa [ˈcɛːva] 'give', because Icelandic lenis stops are voiceless; it contrasts with aspirated [cʰ] from k.

examples.from: brgyud 'to pass through, be transmitted', Old Tibetan /*brɡʲut/

examples.note: The source sound is orthographic g followed by the medial y, reconstructed as palatalized *ɡʲ; Amdo dialects keep a voiced palatal (Zêkog /wɟja/ 'hundred').
Initial g before a front unrounded vowel is the unaspirated palatal [c]; before back vowels it stays velar [k], as in gaf [ˈkaːf] 'gave'.
Faroese gestur shows the affricate [t͡ʃ] instead.
